title: Endless Jailbreaks with Bijection Learning

contributions.purpose: Produce a black-box jailbreak attack that is universal and generates an effectively endless supply of attack prompts for any single harmful intent, rather than relying on a fixed hand-crafted cipher set.
contributions.mechanism: Bijection learning: teach the target LLM an arbitrary randomly-generated string-to-string encoding ('bijection language') in-context, pass the encoded harmful query so it bypasses safety training, then apply the inverse mapping (plus a GPT-4o-mini denoiser to fix decoding errors) to recover the response. Random sampling of encodings enables best-of-n over many prompts.
contributions.evaluation: State-of-the-art ASR across GPT and Claude frontier models on AdvBench and HarmBench, outperforming the ensemble of previous encoding attacks by >=30 percentage points; 86.3% ASR against Claude 3.5 Sonnet on HarmBench. Best-of-n more than doubles single-attempt ASR on all models.
contributions.source_quote: Bijection learning uses random sampling to generate encodings, which allows for best-of-n sampling among a potentially endless quantity of jailbreak prompts for a single harmful intent. Our method generalizes from previous encoding-based jailbreaks, which use a limited, usually hand-crafted collection of ciphers or languages to encode the attack intent.

contributions.purpose: Make an encoding-based jailbreak scale-adaptive, so it can be tuned to any model capability level rather than working only on models that already know a specific fixed cipher.
contributions.mechanism: Introduce quantitative complexity hyperparameters (e.g. number of key-value mappings in the bijection) that smoothly control encoding complexity, allowing fine-grained adaptation of the attack to the target model's capability.
contributions.evaluation: First in the jailbreaking literature to use hyperparameters to scale encoding complexity; enables smooth control vs the discontinuous efficacy gaps of prior encoding attacks. Attack is characterized as black-box, universal, and scale-adaptive.
contributions.source_quote: We are the first in the jailbreaking literature to use quantitative hyperparameters to scale encoding complexity... In contrast, our sampling method enables our attack to be uniquely scale-adaptive, since we control encoding complexity in a smooth, fine-grained manner to adapt jailbreak prompts to varying levels of model capability.

contributions.purpose: Establish the scientific finding that increased model capability itself is a vulnerability: more capable models are more severely jailbroken.
contributions.mechanism: Correlation/scaling analysis plotting bijection complexity against model scale (MMLU capability vs HarmBench ASR) across Claude, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 families; plus analysis of guardrail failures.
contributions.evaluation: Reveals a Pareto frontier of model vulnerability with a two-stage scaling/saturated regime (ASR peaks at intermediate complexity); attack efficacy follows per-model and cross-model scaling laws (Gemini is an exception with no turning point). Provides evidence attacks succeed by making safety-guardrail classification difficult: a Sonnet guardrail only cuts ASR by 10pp while tripling inference cost.
contributions.source_quote: Comparing bijection complexity and model scale reveals a Pareto frontier of model vulnerability... Our work highlights that new vulnerabilities in frontier models can emerge with scale: more capable models are more severely jailbroken by bijection attacks.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Previous work has explored the use of languages and/or encodings to obfuscate harmful prompts, including low-resource languages (Yong et al., 2023), common encodings (Yuan et al., 2024) including ASCII (Jiang et al., 2024), Morse code (Barak, 2023), and other ciphers (Wei et al., 2023; Handa et al., 2024)... However, our work is the first to harness frontier models' ability to learn encodings in-context rather than relying on their intrinsic knowledge to interpret memorized encodings.
Recent work also showed that allowing fine-tuning access enables attackers to teach models complex ciphers with which to evade safety detection (Halawi et al., 2024).
In this work, we unify these two directions in the jailbreaking literature to produce powerful evidence that increased model capabilities give rise to distinct emergent model vulnerabilities.

notes: Attack paper; results are uniformly positive for the attack (high ASR). Trade-off / caveat signals worth noting: (1) the defended-system result is a partial-mitigation caveat - a Sonnet guardrail reduces ASR by only 10 percentage points while TRIPLING inference cost, i.e. defense is expensive and weak. (2) Authors flag that prior LLM-judge ASR metrics are noisy/false-positive-prone and build their own denoiser+judge. (3) Gemini models are an explicit exception to the two-stage scaling law. Method is explicitly framed as generalizing prior encoding-based jailbreaks (Yong 2023, Yuan 2024, Wei 2023, Halawi 2024) by moving from fixed memorized ciphers to in-context-learned random bijections.
